Difficult Observations: Diagnostics, ROBPCA, Cellwise PCA, Sparse PCA, and RPCA

v04-diagnostics-robust-sparse-rpca.Rmd

Difficult Observations: Diagnostics, ROBPCA, Cellwise PCA, Sparse PCA, and RPCA

Package: pcaLab
Target version: 0.1.0
Role in the vignette system: Observation diagnostics and four distinct responses to difficult data: casewise robustness, cellwise robustness, sparse loading structures, and low-rank plus sparse decomposition.

This source is intentionally instructional. It is not precompiled here. Code that requires an optional backend is guarded in the examples or should be run only after pca_capabilities() confirms availability.

Learning objectives

The reader will learn to:

  1. distinguish score distance, orthogonal distance, leverage, and reconstruction residuals;
  2. classify regular observations, good leverage points, orthogonal outliers, and bad leverage points;
  3. avoid treating every flagged point as a data error;
  4. use casewise ROBPCA when whole observations are contaminated;
  5. use cellwise methods when only selected measurements are corrupted;
  6. use sparse PCA for interpretability rather than pretending it is the same optimization problem as ordinary PCA;
  7. combine robustness and sparsity when both are scientifically justified;
  8. distinguish ROBPCA from Principal Component Pursuit / RPCA and interpret low-rank plus sparse decompositions correctly;
  9. compare subspaces rather than comparing arbitrary loading signs.

Scope and relationship to the other vignettes

This vignette is intentionally focused. It develops the topics below in depth and avoids reproducing material assigned to other blocks.

Developed here: Observation diagnostics and four distinct responses to difficult data: casewise robustness, cellwise robustness, sparse loading structures, and low-rank plus sparse decomposition.

Not developed here: Missing-data imputation, probabilistic latent-variable models, generalized PCA, and compositional geometry are not repeated here.

Part V. Diagnostics and difficult observations

19. Diagnose observations before calling them outliers

PCA is sensitive to observations that are extreme in the component space, poorly reconstructed by the retained subspace, or both.

pca_diagnose() reports:

  • score distance;
  • orthogonal distance;
  • leverage;
  • score-distance cutoff when a defensible Euclidean reference exists;
  • orthogonal-distance cutoff;
  • observation-level flags.
diag <- pca_diagnose(
  fit,
  level = 0.975
)

head(diag)
subset(diag, outlier_flag)

Publication figure:

p_diag <- pca_plot(
  fit,
  type = "diagnostics"
)

p_diag

19.1 Score distance

Score distance asks whether an observation is extreme within the retained component space.

Conceptually, for an ordinary PCA with component variances λk\lambda_k,

SDi2=∑k=1Ktik2λk. SD_i^2 = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{t_{ik}^2}{\lambda_k}.

19.2 Orthogonal distance

Orthogonal distance measures how far an observation lies from its low-rank reconstruction:

ODi=∥𝒙i−𝒙̂i,K∥. OD_i = \left\|\mathbf x_i - \widehat{\mathbf x}_{i,K}\right\|.

19.3 Four useful diagnostic categories

Score distance Orthogonal distance Interpretation
low low regular observation well represented by retained PCs
high low extreme within the modeled PC space, but still well represented
low high poorly reconstructed observation that does not follow the dominant structure
high high extreme and poorly represented; investigate carefully

19.4 What not to do

Do not automatically remove a flagged observation.

Instead:

  1. verify data entry and measurement provenance;
  2. identify whether the point belongs to a legitimate treatment, environment, genotype, or rare biological state;
  3. determine whether the problem is casewise or cellwise;
  4. compare classical and appropriate robust analyses;
  5. report sensitivity if the scientific conclusion changes.

Part VI. Robust, sparse, and low-rank alternatives

20. Casewise robust PCA: whole observations are contaminated

Create a known-contamination simulation:

sim_case <- pca_simulate(
  n = 180,
  p = 10,
  rank = 3,
  noise = 0.35,
  casewise = 0.08,
  seed = 1001
)

length(sim_case$casewise_outliers)
sim_case$casewise_outliers

Fit ordinary PCA:

fit_case_classic <- pca_fit(
  sim_case$data,
  method = "classical",
  center = TRUE,
  scale = TRUE,
  ncomp = 3
)

Fit ROBPCA when rospca is available:

if (requireNamespace("rospca", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit_case_robust <- pca_fit(
    sim_case$data,
    method = "robust",
    center = TRUE,
    scale = TRUE,
    ncomp = 3,
    alpha = 0.75
  )

  fit_case_robust
  pca_plot(fit_case_robust, type = "diagnostics")
}

20.1 Compare the recovered subspaces 

if (exists("fit_case_robust")) {
  cmp_case <- pca_compare(
    list(
      classical = fit_case_classic,
      robust = fit_case_robust
    ),
    ncomp = 3
  )

  cmp_case$metrics
  cmp_case$subspace_angles
}

Interpretation

Casewise robust PCA is appropriate when whole rows can be atypical. It should not be described simply as “PCA after deleting outliers.” The robust fit estimates the dominant subspace using procedures designed to resist contamination.

A material difference between classical and robust subspaces is evidence that the ordinary PCA geometry is sensitive to a subset of observations. The next step is scientific investigation of those observations, not automatic exclusion.

21. Cellwise robust PCA: only some measurements are corrupted

In high-dimensional laboratory or sensor data, a row can be mostly valid while one or two cells are contaminated.

sim_cell <- pca_simulate(
  n = 160,
  p = 18,
  rank = 3,
  noise = 0.30,
  cellwise = 0.03,
  seed = 1002
)

head(sim_cell$cellwise_outliers)

If cellWise is installed:

if (requireNamespace("cellWise", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit_cell <- pca_fit(
    sim_cell$data,
    method = "cellwise",
    center = TRUE,
    scale = TRUE,
    ncomp = 3
  )

  fit_cell
  pca_plot(fit_cell, type = "diagnostics")
}

Interpretation

Casewise ROBPCA and MacroPCA answer different contamination problems.

If only a few spectral channels, chemical assays, or sensor readings are corrupted, classifying the entire plot or plant as an outlier can discard valid information. A cellwise method can preserve usable measurements while reducing the influence of contaminated cells.

22. Sparse PCA: simplify the loading structure

Ordinary PCs typically involve every measured variable. In metabolomics, spectroscopy, genomics, soil chemistry, or high-dimensional phenotyping, that can make interpretation difficult.

Simulate a moderate-dimensional problem:

sim_sparse <- pca_simulate(
  n = 220,
  p = 30,
  rank = 3,
  noise = 0.40,
  seed = 1003
)

Classical reference:

fit_sparse_ref <- pca_fit(
  sim_sparse$data,
  method = "classical",
  center = TRUE,
  scale = TRUE,
  ncomp = 3
)

Sparse PCA with sparsepca:

if (requireNamespace("sparsepca", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit_sparse <- pca_fit(
    sim_sparse$data,
    method = "sparse",
    center = TRUE,
    scale = TRUE,
    ncomp = 3,
    backend = "sparsepca",
    alpha = 1e-4,
    beta = 1e-4
  )

  fit_sparse$extra$sparsity
  pca_plot(fit_sparse, type = "loadings", component = 1)
}

Alternative elasticnet backend:

if (requireNamespace("elasticnet", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit_sparse_en <- pca_fit(
    sim_sparse$data,
    method = "sparse",
    center = TRUE,
    scale = TRUE,
    ncomp = 3,
    backend = "elasticnet",
    cardinality = c(8, 8, 8)
  )
}

Interpretation

Sparse PCA deliberately trades some fidelity for simpler loading structure. It can make a component easier to explain, but sparsity itself does not guarantee that the retained variables are scientifically important or statistically stable.

Compare:

  • reconstruction error;
  • loading sparsity;
  • subspace orientation;
  • bootstrap stability where a faithful refit is available;
  • scientific interpretability.

23. Robust sparse PCA: interpretability under contamination

When both contamination and dense loading structure are problems, robust sparse PCA can combine resistance and sparsity.

sim_rs <- pca_simulate(
  n = 200,
  p = 25,
  rank = 3,
  noise = 0.35,
  casewise = 0.05,
  seed = 1004
)
if (requireNamespace("rospca", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit_rs <- pca_fit(
    sim_rs$data,
    method = "robust_sparse",
    center = TRUE,
    scale = TRUE,
    ncomp = 3,
    backend = "rospca",
    lambda = 0.20,
    alpha = 0.75
  )

  pca_plot(fit_rs, type = "loadings", component = 1)
}

Interpretation

A sparse robust loading vector can be easier to communicate, but its zeros are method-dependent regularized estimates. Do not interpret an exact zero as proof that a variable has no biological relationship with the latent process.

24. RPCA/PCP: low-rank signal plus sparse corruption

pcaLab separates Principal Component Pursuit from casewise ROBPCA.

The decomposition is

𝑿=𝑳+𝑺+𝑬, \mathbf X = \mathbf L + \mathbf S + \mathbf E,

where:

  • 𝑳\mathbf L is low rank;
  • 𝑺\mathbf S is sparse corruption;
  • 𝑬\mathbf E represents any remaining small residual error conceptually.

The internal implementation estimates a low-rank and sparse decomposition through an inexact augmented-Lagrangian style algorithm.

sim_rpca <- pca_simulate(
  n = 160,
  p = 24,
  rank = 3,
  noise = 0.10,
  cellwise = 0.04,
  seed = 1005
)

fit_rpca <- pca_fit(
  sim_rpca$data,
  method = "rpca",
  center = TRUE,
  scale = FALSE,
  ncomp = 3
)

fit_rpca$extra$converged
fit_rpca$extra$iterations
fit_rpca$extra$relative_residual

Inspect the low-rank and sparse matrices:

L <- fit_rpca$extra$low_rank
S <- fit_rpca$extra$sparse

dim(L)
dim(S)

mean(abs(S) > 1e-8)

Interpretation

RPCA/PCP is not merely a “more robust PCA.” It assumes a specific decomposition of the observed matrix into low-rank signal and sparse additive corruption. Use it when that matrix model is scientifically plausible.

60. Using ROBPCA for cellwise corruption

Casewise and cellwise contamination are different problems.

Use:

pca_fit(method = "robust")
pca_fit(method = "cellwise")

according to the contamination mechanism.

61. Calling RPCA/PCP and ROBPCA the same method

They solve different mathematical problems.

pca_fit(method = "rpca")
pca_fit(method = "robust")

The first decomposes a matrix into low-rank and sparse parts. The second estimates a resistant principal subspace under rowwise contamination.

Where to continue

Continue to 05-missing-probabilistic-high-dimensional.Rmd if incompleteness or p >> n is the primary challenge.

Reproducibility note

The examples use package-generated or explicitly simulated teaching data. They demonstrate workflow and interpretation, not empirical evidence. For stochastic procedures, set and report a seed. For optional engines, record backend versions with sessionInfo() and preserve the preprocessing specification used to create the fitted object.
